sections.title: The organism and how it causes disease

blocks.text: **Enteric fever** is the umbrella name for two closely related illnesses: **typhoid fever**, caused by _Salmonella_ **Typhi**, and **paratyphoid fever**, caused by _Salmonella_ **Paratyphi**. Davidson names Paratyphi **A and B**; Kumar & Clark and K&C Essentials also list **type C**. Paratyphoid looks like typhoid but is usually the milder of the two.

blocks.title: Pathogenesis in steps
items: The swallowed organism crosses the **small-bowel wall through Peyer’s patches**.
It spreads to the **regional lymph nodes** and from there enters the **bloodstream**.
After a few days of bacteraemia the bacilli **settle in small-intestinal lymphoid tissue** (Peyer’s patches and lymphoid follicles).
These lesions first **swell**, then **ulcerate**, and usually heal. The ulcers explain the later **bleeding and perforation**.
Salmonella can invade enterocytes, giving both a secretory diarrhoea and **invasive systemic disease**. Systemic spread is the hallmark of Typhi and Paratyphi.

blocks.title: Typhoidal vs non-typhoidal Salmonella
rows: Food sources such as eggs, poultry and milk; also hamsters
Self-limiting diarrhoea and vomiting (enterocolitis); a cause of travellers’ diarrhoea
In 5–10%; up to a third of bacteraemic patients over 50 may develop aortitis
Occasional, mainly in the immunocompromised and the elderly

blocks.text: **Humans are the only natural host of S. Typhi.** There is no animal source, so every case comes from another person: either someone acutely ill or a **carrier**.

Do not label every Salmonella infection as typhoid. Food-borne **non-typhoidal** species (S. Enteritidis, S. Choleraesuis) mostly cause a short, self-limiting gastroenteritis. That is a separate entity from enteric fever.

Typhoid spreads by the **faecal–oral route**, through **contaminated food or water**. It thrives where housing is **overcrowded and sanitation poor**. Davidson’s main endemic regions are **South Asia (the Indian subcontinent), Africa south of the Sahara and Latin America**; elsewhere it is uncommon. Kumar estimates **over 17 million cases and about 150 000 deaths a year**, mostly in India and Africa.

blocks.title: Typical patient in an exam vignette
items: A **returned traveller** from South or South-east Asia, sub-Saharan Africa, Central or South America, or the Caribbean and Mexico.
A traveller who drank **unpurified water** or who was **not immunised**.
Alongside malaria, viral hepatitis and dengue, typhoid is one of the **commonest final diagnoses** in fever after tropical travel.

blocks.title: Carriers: the reservoir that keeps typhoid going
rows: Keeps shedding S. Typhi for several months after recovery
Still excreting the organism **more than 1 year** after recovery
Gallbladder; shedding is **intermittent**, mainly in stool and less often in urine
Common where **urinary schistosomiasis** occurs (parts of the Middle East and Africa)

blocks.title: Prevention
items: Better **sanitation, living conditions and safe water** cut the incidence.
Travellers should avoid **untreated water, ice in drinks and ice cream**.
Three vaccines are available to travellers: **two inactivated injectable vaccines and one oral live attenuated vaccine**. All give only **partial protection**.
A newer **conjugate vaccine** gives stronger, longer-lasting immunity. With GAVI funding, it was due to be rolled out to children in endemic countries from 2019.

blocks.text: Enteric fever (typhoid or paratyphoid) is a **notifiable disease** under the UK regulations and a reportable disease more widely. Public health officials must be told, even when this overrides confidentiality.

**Carrier rates differ between the books.** Davidson says about **5%** become chronic carriers. Kumar gives up to 10% convalescent carriers and **1–4%** chronic carriers. Quote Davidson’s figure, and define chronic carriage as **excretion beyond 1 year**.

The **incubation period** is usually about **10–14 days**, though it can be longer, and the onset is often **insidious**. K&C Essentials also gives a 5–21-day range and puts enteric fever in the "medium" (10–21 days) incubation group.

blocks.title: Typhoid fever by week of illness
rows: Fever rising in a **stepladder** pattern over 4–5 days; malaise, worsening headache, drowsiness, limb aches, dry cough; **relative bradycardia**; **constipation** in adults; **diarrhoea and vomiting** in children

**Rose spots** on the trunk; **splenomegaly** (palpable around days 7–10); hepatomegaly and cervical lymph nodes (Kumar, K&C Essentials); cough and epistaxis; constipation gives way to **diarrhoea** with abdominal distension and tenderness; bronchitis or delirium may follow
Complications such as gut **haemorrhage** and **perforation**. Without treatment: delirium, coma and death

blocks.title: Rose spots
items: Sparse, **slightly raised, rose-red** spots that **blanch** when pressed.
They sit on the **upper abdomen, chest and back**.
They appear at the **end of the first week** and are usually seen only on **white skin**.
Kumar calls the rash **scanty** and maculopapular.

blocks.text: **Paratyphoid fever** is **shorter and milder** than typhoid. It tends to start **suddenly**, often as an acute enteritis. Rose spots can be **more plentiful**, while gut complications are **rarer**.

blocks.title: Where typhoid turns up in differential lists
items: Fever in a traveller with **CNS involvement**, and fever with **rash**.
It can present **within 2 weeks** of return or **more than 6 weeks** later.
It is an infectious cause of **fever of unknown origin**.
It is an acute infection that gives **moderate (not massive) splenomegaly**.
Like meningococcal disease, it is a severe infection that can cause an **acquired vascular bleeding disorder**.

blocks.text: Exam keyword pattern: **fever + constipation + rose-spot rash + relative bradycardia = typhoid**. Relative bradycardia means the pulse is slower than you would expect for the height of the fever.

In adults the early bowel symptom is usually **constipation**, caused by swollen lymphoid tissue around the ileocaecal junction. Diarrhoea comes later. **Children** may have diarrhoea and vomiting from the start.

blocks.title: Complications of typhoid
rows: Bone and joint infection (osteomyelitis), meningitis, cholecystitis

blocks.text: Because bacteraemia in week 1 seeds the whole body, almost **any organ** can be involved. Davidson puts gut bleeding and perforation at the **end of week 2 or during week 3**. Kumar and K&C Essentials say complications **usually arise in week 3**. They can occur without treatment and, occasionally, even after it.

blocks.title: Prognosis
items: Where healthcare is limited, **up to 30%** of patients die and **10% of untreated survivors relapse**.
In the USA, by comparison, mortality is about **1–2%**.
Even effective treatment does not remove the risk of complications, **recrudescence** or a **carrier state**.

blocks.text: **Children with sickle-cell disease** often develop **bone and joint infection** with typhoid.
Typhoid is one of the infections that can cause **acalculous cholecystitis**: gallbladder inflammation from stasis and ischaemia, without stones.
In week 2–3, a sudden fall in temperature to **normal or subnormal** can be falsely reassuring. It may mean **intestinal haemorrhage**, not recovery.
**Which week does haemorrhage occur?** Davidson says the end of week 2 or week 3; Kumar and K&C Essentials say usually week 3. Past papers ask this question, and **week 3** satisfies every source.

In **week 1** the patient has a generalised bacteraemic illness with **no localising signs**, so diagnosis is difficult. A **leucopenia** is typical but non-specific. In tropically acquired fever without localising signs and with a **normal white cell count**, think of **malaria, typhoid and typhus**. For typhoid, send **blood and stool cultures**.

blocks.title: Culture is the diagnostic standard
rows: Positive in most cases in the **first 2 weeks**
**Establishes the diagnosis**; taking several sets raises the yield
A positive stool may reflect **chronic carriage** rather than acute infection
Depends on the stage at presentation
When the diagnosis is in doubt, or after **antibiotics have already been given**
**Picks up more cases than blood culture** and can stay positive on antibiotics. In PUO, send marrow for culture as well as microscopy

blocks.title: Work-up of a febrile returned traveller
items: **Exclude malaria first**: a rapid antigen test plus thick and thin films, at least three sets in total.
FBC with differential, U&E, LFTs and glucose.
Blood cultures, plus urine and stool cultures.
Chest X-ray, liver and spleen ultrasound, and an HIV test.
Bone marrow aspirate is one of the targeted second-line tests.

blocks.text: A febrile traveller from a malaria area has **malaria until proven otherwise**, and **one negative smear does not exclude it**. Rule out malaria before settling on enteric fever.

**The Widal test** is an agglutination test for antibodies to the **O and H antigens** of S. Typhi and Paratyphi. Davidson calls it **not specific**, though some regions still use it. Kumar goes further: it has little practical value, is easily misread and should not be used. **Culture, not Widal**, confirms typhoid.

Routine antibiotics are not used for simple gastroenteritis, but they **are indicated in invasive salmonellosis, especially typhoid**. The choice of drug must be **guided by in vitro sensitivity testing**, because resistance is widespread.

blocks.title: Antibiotics in enteric fever
rows: **Drug of choice** when a **nalidixic acid screen** suggests the isolate is susceptible. Resistance is frequent, notably in isolates from the Indian subcontinent and in the UK
Useful alternatives with a slightly **higher treatment-failure rate**. K&C Essentials uses IV ceftriaxone first-line until fluoroquinolone sensitivity is known
Alternative when there is **fluoroquinolone resistance**; **not validated in severe disease**. K&C Essentials: for uncomplicated disease
With azithromycin, the only drugs still effective against **XDR typhoid** (Kumar)
500 mg 4× daily; 750 mg 4× daily; 2 tablets twice daily
Older agents **failing through resistance**, especially in India and South-east Asia

blocks.title: Resistance labels (Kumar)
rows: Spreading fast: in Malawi it rose from 7% of isolates in 2010 to 97% in 2014
Increasingly common, notably in **Pakistan**; only **azithromycin and carbapenems** still work

blocks.title: Course and response
items: Treat for **14 days** in total. A full course lowers the risk of relapse and persistent carriage.
Fever may continue for **up to 5 days** after effective therapy starts. On its own, this is **not treatment failure**.
Even after good treatment, complications, recrudescence and carriage can still occur.

blocks.title: Chronic carriers
items: Carriers need a **prolonged antibiotic course**.
**Ciprofloxacin for 4 weeks** was the traditional regimen. Today the drug and duration may need to follow sensitivity testing.
Prolonged antibiotics **rarely clear carriage when the gallbladder is diseased** (Kumar).
**Cholecystectomy may be necessary** (Davidson).

blocks.text: **First-line drug: the books differ.** Davidson makes a **fluoroquinolone** the drug of choice when nalidixic acid screening predicts susceptibility, with cephalosporins as alternatives. K&C Essentials starts **IV ceftriaxone** until fluoroquinolone sensitivity is known. Follow Davidson, and remember that both make **sensitivity testing** decide the final drug.
**Cholecystectomy for carriers:** Davidson says it may be necessary; Kumar says it is not usually justified on clinical or public health grounds. Answer with Davidson’s view.

cards.front: Which organisms cause typhoid and paratyphoid fever?
cards.back: Typhoid: **Salmonella Typhi**. Paratyphoid: **Salmonella Paratyphi A and B** (Kumar and K&C Essentials add C).

cards.front: How does S. Typhi get from the gut into the blood?
cards.back: It crosses the small-bowel wall through **Peyer’s patches**, travels to the **regional lymph nodes**, then enters the **bloodstream**.

cards.front: What is the natural host of S. Typhi?
cards.back: **Humans only.** There is no animal reservoir.
By the **faecal–oral route**, through contaminated **food or water**.

cards.front: How is a chronic typhoid carrier defined, how common is it, and where does the organism persist?
cards.back: Still excreting the organism **more than 1 year** after recovery. About **5%** of patients (Davidson). The usual site is the **gallbladder**, often with gallstones.

cards.front: Where can chronic S. Typhi carriage occur in areas with urinary schistosomiasis?
Which typhoid vaccines are available to travellers, and how well do they protect?
cards.back: Two **inactivated injectable** vaccines and one **oral live attenuated** vaccine. All give only **partial protection**.

cards.front: What fever pattern is typical in week 1 of typhoid?
cards.back: A **stepladder** rise over 4–5 days, with headache, malaise and limb aches.
A **pulse slower than expected** for the height of the fever. It is a classic sign of typhoid.

cards.front: Describe rose spots: what they look like, where and when they appear.
cards.back: Sparse, slightly raised, **rose-red spots that blanch** on pressure. They appear on the **upper abdomen and back** at the **end of week 1**.

cards.front: When do gut haemorrhage and perforation occur in typhoid, and what sign can mislead you?
cards.back: At the **end of week 2 or in week 3**. A **fall in temperature** during intestinal bleeding can be falsely reassuring.

cards.front: Which typhoid complication is common in children with sickle-cell disease?
Which test establishes the diagnosis of typhoid?
cards.back: **Blood culture**, ideally several sets. Stool culture is often positive in weeks 2–3.

cards.front: When is bone marrow culture useful in typhoid?
cards.back: When the diagnosis is in doubt, especially **after antibiotics have been given**. It picks up **more cases than blood culture** does.

cards.front: What is Davidson’s drug of choice for typhoid?
cards.back: A **fluoroquinolone** such as ciprofloxacin (500 mg twice daily), provided a **nalidixic acid screen** suggests the isolate is susceptible.

cards.front: Which drugs still work against XDR typhoid?
How long is typhoid treated, and how long may fever continue after effective therapy starts?
cards.back: Treat for **14 days**. Fever may continue for **up to 5 days** after starting therapy.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man has just returned from 3 weeks in rural Bangladesh. For 9 days he has had a fever that climbed higher each day, with headache and constipation. His temperature is 39.8 °C and his pulse is 84/min.
questions.leadIn: Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: A stepladder fever with constipation and a pulse that is slow for the temperature (relative bradycardia), in a traveller from the Indian subcontinent, is classic **typhoid**. The cause is **S. Typhi**, an organism whose only natural host is humans.
whyNot: A non-typhoidal Salmonella. It usually causes a short, self-limiting bout of diarrhoea and vomiting, often from eggs or poultry, not a 9-day systemic fever.
Also a non-typhoidal Salmonella, listed with enterocolitis rather than enteric fever.
Causes dysentery-type diarrhoea. It does not explain a stepladder fever with constipation and relative bradycardia.
A diarrhoeal pathogen. It does not fit this enteric-fever picture.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman with untreated typhoid is in her third week of illness. She suddenly develops severe abdominal pain, and her abdomen becomes rigid. At laparotomy the surgeon finds a perforated ulcer.
questions.leadIn: In which tissue did the ulcer most likely arise?
options: Lymphoid tissue (Peyer’s patches) of the small intestine
Mucosa of the rectum and sigmoid colon
questions.explanation: After bacteraemia, typhoid bacilli settle in **small-intestinal lymphoid tissue**. Peyer’s patches **swell, then ulcerate**, and these ulcers can **bleed or perforate** at the end of week 2 or in week 3.
whyNot: Typhoid lesions do not form in the stomach.
The lesions are in small-bowel lymphoid tissue, not the distal colon.
Peptic ulcers form here; typhoid ulcers form in Peyer’s patches further down the small bowel.
This is not a site of typhoid ulceration.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old cook had typhoid 18 months ago and has been well since. Routine screening finds S. Typhi in her stool on some occasions but not others. An ultrasound shows gallstones.
questions.leadIn: Where is the organism most likely persisting?
questions.explanation: She is a **chronic carrier**: still excreting more than 1 year after recovery. The usual reservoir is the **gallbladder**, which explains the **intermittent** shedding in stool and the link with **gallstones**.
whyNot: Bladder carriage occurs mainly where urinary schistosomiasis is common, and it would give shedding in urine. She has gallstones and organisms in her stool.
Marrow is a sensitive site for diagnostic culture in acute illness, not the usual carrier reservoir.
The spleen enlarges during acute illness but is not the site of carriage.
The lymph nodes are involved in early spread, not in long-term carriage.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman is planning a backpacking trip to rural Pakistan. She asks how people catch typhoid.
questions.leadIn: What is the main route of transmission?
options: Faecal–oral, through contaminated food or water
The bite of an infected mosquito
Skin contact with fresh water contaminated by animal urine
questions.explanation: Typhoid spreads by the **faecal–oral route** in **contaminated food or water**. Humans are the only host, so the source is always another person’s faeces or urine. That is why travellers are told to avoid **untreated water, ice and ice cream**.
whyNot: Typhoid has no insect vector. Mosquito-borne fevers are a different group.
Typhoid is not an airborne infection.
Freshwater exposure is a risk for other infections, such as leptospirosis. S. Typhi has no animal reservoir.
Milk-borne zoonoses come from animals. S. Typhi infects only humans.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man returned from Nepal 2 weeks ago. He is on day 6 of a fever, with headache and constipation. His temperature is 39.9 °C.
questions.leadIn: Which examination finding would most strongly support typhoid?
options: A pulse rate inappropriately slow for the fever
Massive splenomegaly reaching the right iliac fossa
Neck stiffness with a positive Kernig’s sign
A tender, enlarged liver with basal lung crackles
questions.explanation: **Relative bradycardia**, a pulse slower than the fever would predict, is a classic sign of typhoid in week 1. Combined with fever, constipation and a rash, it forms the textbook pattern.
whyNot: Typhoid causes moderate splenomegaly, palpable from about days 7–10, not massive splenomegaly.
Rose spots blanch on pressure. A non-blanching rash points elsewhere.
Meningitis is a later complication, not a feature of week 1.
This combination is the keyword pattern for amoebic liver abscess, not typhoid.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old student is on day 8 of a febrile illness that began after a trip to Peru. Examination shows a few slightly raised pink spots on the upper abdomen and back. They fade when pressed.
questions.leadIn: What are these lesions most likely to be?
questions.explanation: Sparse, slightly raised, **rose-red spots that blanch**, on the **upper abdomen and back** at the **end of week 1**, are **rose spots**. They are usually visible only on white skin.
whyNot: These are tender nodules, typically on the shins, not sparse blanching spots on the trunk.
Purpura does not blanch.
An eschar is a single dark scab at a bite site, not scattered pink spots.
Wheals are itchy and come and go; they are not a timed sign at the end of week 1.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man is in the third week of typhoid. Overnight his temperature falls from 39.5 °C to 36.1 °C. At the same time his pulse rises to 118/min and he passes dark, tarry stools.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely explanation for the change in temperature?
options: Intestinal haemorrhage from ulcerated Peyer’s patches
Recovery as the fever settles naturally
questions.explanation: Bleeding from ulcerated Peyer’s patches occurs at the **end of week 2 or in week 3**. A drop in temperature to normal or subnormal during **intestinal haemorrhage** can be **falsely reassuring**. Tachycardia and melaena give it away.
whyNot: A falling temperature with tachycardia and melaena is not recovery. This is the trap the books warn about.
Relapse brings a return of fever, not a sudden drop with melaena.
Cholecystitis is a septic complication but would not cause melaena with an abrupt fall in temperature.
Myocarditis is a toxic complication. It does not explain tarry stools.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with sickle-cell disease is in the third week of confirmed typhoid. He develops a painful, swollen lower leg and will not bear weight.
questions.leadIn: Which complication is most likely?
questions.explanation: **Bone and joint infection** (osteomyelitis) is a septic-focus complication of typhoid and is **common in children with sickle-cell disease**.
whyNot: A toxic cardiac complication. It does not cause a painful, swollen limb.
A toxic renal complication. It does not cause a painful, swollen limb.
This gives an acute abdomen, not limb signs.
This gives headache and neck stiffness, not a swollen leg.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man returned from India 10 days ago. He has had fever for 5 days with no localising signs. You suspect typhoid.
questions.leadIn: Which investigation is most likely to confirm the diagnosis at this stage?
questions.explanation: In the first 2 weeks **blood culture** is positive in most cases and **establishes the diagnosis**. Taking several sets raises the yield.
whyNot: The Widal test is not specific and cannot confirm typhoid.
Stool cultures are more often positive in weeks 2–3, and a positive result may reflect carriage.
Urine can grow the organism depending on the stage of illness, but blood culture is the test that establishes the diagnosis in the first 2 weeks.
Leucopenia is typical but non-specific. It supports the diagnosis but cannot confirm it.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman returned from Nepal with 2 weeks of fever. Before travelling home she took a course of antibiotics from a local pharmacy. Three blood cultures are now negative, but typhoid is still strongly suspected.
questions.leadIn: Which investigation is most likely to give the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: **Bone marrow culture** detects more infections than blood culture and can stay positive **after antibiotics have been started**. That is exactly when it is needed.
whyNot: Serology is non-specific and should not be relied on.
A low white count is non-specific.
Imaging may show organ enlargement but cannot identify the organism.
A dipstick does not culture S. Typhi.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man in the UK has blood-culture-proven typhoid. He is not severely ill. Nalidixic acid screening of his isolate predicts fluoroquinolone susceptibility.
questions.leadIn: Which antibiotic does Davidson recommend as the drug of choice?
questions.explanation: Davidson makes a **fluoroquinolone** such as **ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily** the drug of choice when **nalidixic acid screening predicts susceptibility**. Sensitivity testing should always guide the choice.
whyNot: An older agent that is failing because of resistance, especially in India and South-east Asia.
An older agent that is losing effect because of resistance.
An older agent that is losing effect because of resistance.
Kept for fluoroquinolone resistance. It is not validated in severe disease.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with typhoid is on day 3 of ciprofloxacin. Her isolate is fully sensitive to it. She is haemodynamically stable with no abdominal signs, but she still has a fever of 38.8 °C.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Stop antibiotics because the fever must be drug-induced
questions.explanation: Fever can continue for **up to 5 days** after effective therapy starts. On its own, this is **not treatment failure**. Continue the sensitive drug for a full **14-day** course.
whyNot: There is no evidence of resistance. Chloramphenicol is an older drug that is losing effect.
A sensitive isolate with an expected fever lag does not need a second drug.
Persistent fever is expected early in treatment, and stopping risks relapse.
Cholecystectomy is considered for chronic carriers, not for acute typhoid on day 3.

questions.theme: Fever and gut symptoms after travel
questions.leadIn: Match each traveller below to the single most likely diagnosis in the list. Any option can be the answer for one case, several cases or none.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman returned from Bangladesh 12 days ago. Her fever has risen a little higher each day for 5 days, with headache and constipation. Her temperature is 39.6 °C and her pulse is 82/min. Her white cell count is low.
items.explanation: Step 1: a **stepladder** fever after travel to the Indian subcontinent suggests enteric fever. Step 2: **constipation** in an adult, a **pulse that is slow for the fever** and **leucopenia** complete the classic week-1 picture of **typhoid**.

items.stem: A 30-year-old man returned from Mexico. His fever began abruptly, with diarrhoea, and has been fairly mild. He has more pink blanching spots on his trunk than his doctor expected. Blood cultures grow an enteric-fever Salmonella, and the laboratory reports that it is **not** serotype Typhi.
items.explanation: Two steps: an enteric-fever Salmonella that is **not Typhi** must be **Paratyphi**. The clinical picture also fits **paratyphoid**: **abrupt onset with enteritis**, a milder and shorter course, and a **heavier crop of rose spots**.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man develops vomiting and diarrhoea after eating undercooked eggs at a barbecue. He has no fever pattern of note, and he recovers fully within a few days without treatment.
items.explanation: Eggs and poultry are typical sources of **non-typhoidal Salmonella**, which causes a **self-limiting** enterocolitis. It is a different entity from enteric fever.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman returned from Ghana 10 days ago with fever and headache. She has no localising signs and a normal white cell count. One blood film is negative. The team is considering typhoid.
items.explanation: A febrile traveller from a malaria zone has **malaria until proven otherwise**, and **one negative smear does not exclude it**. Repeat films and a rapid antigen test are needed before settling on enteric fever.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man returned from Karachi, Pakistan, with blood-culture-proven typhoid. He is now severely unwell, with a high fever and abdominal tenderness. His isolate is resistant to ciprofloxacin and to ceftriaxone.
questions.leadIn: Which antibiotic is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Work it through. **Step 1:** resistance to quinolones **and** third-generation cephalosporins, in a patient from Pakistan, defines **XDR typhoid**. **Step 2:** Kumar says only **azithromycin and carbapenems** still work against XDR typhoid. **Step 3:** Davidson notes that azithromycin is **not validated in severe disease**. In a **severely ill** patient, a **carbapenem** such as meropenem is the safer choice.
whyNot: The isolate is resistant to quinolones.
The isolate is resistant to third-generation cephalosporins.
An older agent that is losing effect through resistance. Against XDR typhoid, only azithromycin and carbapenems are still listed as effective.
Active against XDR strains, but not validated in severe disease. This man is severely ill.

questions.theme: Clinical features and complications of typhoid
questions.leadIn: Match each patient below to the single most likely clinical feature or complication in the list. Any option can be the answer for one case, several cases or none.

items.stem: A 6-year-old girl is on day 4 of confirmed typhoid. Her mother asks which gut symptom is most typical at this early stage in a child of her age.
items.explanation: Two steps: in **adults** the early bowel symptom is constipation, but **children** may have prominent **diarrhoea and vomiting** early in the illness.

items.stem: A 23-year-old man is in week 3 of untreated typhoid. He develops sudden severe abdominal pain. His abdomen is rigid and silent, and an erect chest film shows gas under the diaphragm.
items.explanation: Ulcerated Peyer’s patches can **perforate** at the end of week 2 or in week 3. A rigid abdomen with free gas means **intestinal perforation**.

items.stem: An 8-year-old boy with sickle-cell disease is in week 3 of typhoid. He develops a hot, tender, swollen knee and refuses to walk.
items.explanation: **Bone and joint infection** is a septic-focus complication that is **common in children with sickle-cell disease**.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman is in week 3 of typhoid. Her temperature drops to 36 °C, her pulse climbs to 120/min, and she passes black stools.
items.explanation: A sudden fall in temperature can be **falsely reassuring**. With tachycardia and melaena, it points to **intestinal haemorrhage** from ulcerated Peyer’s patches.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below to the most appropriate next investigation in the list. Any option can be the answer for one case, several cases or none.
options: Malaria rapid antigen test with thick and thin films
Nalidixic acid screening of the isolate

items.stem: A 29-year-old man returned from India a week ago. He has had 4 days of fever with no localising signs. Malaria tests are negative, and you want to confirm suspected typhoid.
items.explanation: **Blood culture** establishes the diagnosis and is positive in most cases in the first 2 weeks. **Several sets** increase the yield.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman with suspected typhoid had already taken a full course of antibiotics before she reached hospital. Repeated blood cultures are sterile, and the diagnosis is still uncertain.
items.explanation: **Marrow culture** finds more infections than blood culture and can remain positive after antibiotics.

items.stem: A 41-year-old man returned from Malawi 9 days ago with fever and headache. He has no localising signs. Before typhoid is pursued, one diagnosis must be actively excluded.
items.explanation: Two steps: fever after travel to sub-Saharan Africa means **malaria must be excluded first**. Use a rapid antigen test and **at least three** thick and thin films.

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman’s blood culture has grown S. Typhi. Before choosing her antibiotic, the team wants to predict whether ciprofloxacin will work.
items.explanation: Davidson recommends fluoroquinolones when **nalidixic acid screening predicts susceptibility**. Treatment must always follow **in vitro sensitivity testing**.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below to the most appropriate treatment in the list. Any option can be the answer for one case, several cases or none.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman in the UK has uncomplicated typhoid. Nalidixic acid screening of her isolate predicts fluoroquinolone susceptibility.
items.explanation: Davidson: **fluoroquinolones** such as ciprofloxacin are the **drugs of choice** when nalidixic acid screening predicts susceptibility.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man has just arrived back from India and is very unwell with suspected enteric fever. Cultures have been sent, and fluoroquinolone sensitivity is not yet known.
items.explanation: Because fluoroquinolone resistance is rising, K&C Essentials gives **IV ceftriaxone** first-line **until sensitivity is known**. Davidson lists extended-spectrum cephalosporins as useful alternatives.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman returned from Lahore with mild, uncomplicated typhoid. She is managing well at home. Her isolate shows resistance to both quinolones and third-generation cephalosporins.
items.explanation: Two steps: resistance to quinolones and third-generation cephalosporins in a patient from **Pakistan** means **XDR typhoid**, which leaves only azithromycin or a carbapenem. In **uncomplicated** disease, **azithromycin** is suitable.

items.stem: A healthy 25-year-old man has had 2 days of watery diarrhoea after a takeaway meal. He has no fever or other systemic features and is improving.
items.explanation: In **non-specific gastroenteritis**, routine antibiotics do not improve the outcome. They are kept for systemic involvement, immunocompromise or significant comorbidity, and for **invasive** salmonellosis such as typhoid.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below to the most likely organism in the list. Any option can be the answer for one case, several cases or none.

items.stem: A 55-year-old farmer from a part of Africa where urinary schistosomiasis is common had an enteric fever 3 years ago. His urine now intermittently grows the same organism, although he feels well.
items.explanation: Two steps: long-term excretion after an enteric fever means a **chronic carrier**. Where **urinary schistosomiasis** is prevalent, **S. Typhi** carriage can occur in the **urinary bladder**.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man develops diarrhoea after eating undercooked chicken. Blood cultures become positive, and weeks later imaging shows an infected aorta (aortitis).
items.explanation: **Non-typhoidal Salmonella** comes from eggs, poultry and milk. It causes bacteraemia in 5–10% of cases, and **aortitis** can follow in up to a third of bacteraemic patients **over 50**.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman returned from Nepal. Her fever began abruptly, with an acute enteritis, and the illness was shorter and milder than her doctors expected. She had a more extensive rose-spot rash than usual and no intestinal complications.
items.explanation: A milder, shorter enteric fever that starts **suddenly** with **enteritis** and a **heavier rash** is **paratyphoid**.

items.stem: Several guests at a wedding develop a stepladder fever, constipation and relative bradycardia 2 weeks after the event. The outbreak is traced to a caterer who had enteric fever 2 years ago and has gallstones.
items.explanation: The guests have classic **typhoid**. The source is a **chronic gallbladder carrier** of **S. Typhi**: humans are its only host, and carriage is linked with gallstones.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old food handler has gallstones and remains a chronic S. Typhi carrier despite a prolonged course of antibiotics guided by sensitivity testing.
questions.leadIn: According to Davidson, what further option may be necessary?
questions.explanation: Davidson says chronic carriers need prolonged, sensitivity-guided antibiotics, and that **cholecystectomy may be necessary**. Kumar is more doubtful, noting that antibiotics rarely clear carriage when the gallbladder is diseased and that surgery is not usually justified. For exams, follow Davidson.
whyNot: The spleen is not the site of carriage.
Vaccines prevent infection in travellers. They do not clear established carriage.
Carriage needs a prolonged course; a single dose would not clear it.
The appendix is not the reservoir. The gallbladder is.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old is about to spend 3 months volunteering in rural India. She has had a typhoid vaccine and asks what else she can do to reduce her risk of typhoid.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Avoid untreated water, ice in drinks and ice cream
Use insect repellent at dusk and dawn
questions.explanation: Typhoid spreads by the **faecal–oral** route. The vaccines give only **partial protection**, so travellers should still avoid **untreated water, ice and ice cream**.
whyNot: Typhoid has no insect vector.
Freshwater exposure is a risk for other infections, such as schistosomiasis or leptospirosis, not typhoid.
S. Typhi infects only humans, so dogs are not a source.
The cited books list hygiene and vaccination for typhoid prevention, not antibiotic prophylaxis.

questions.leadIn: Match each scenario below to the best time interval or stage in the list. Any option can be the answer for one case, several cases or none.
options: End of the second week to the third week

items.stem: A 26-year-old man drank contaminated water while travelling. If he develops typhoid, the infection is usually silent for about how long before symptoms start?
items.explanation: Davidson gives a typical **incubation period of about 10–14 days**, though it can be longer.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman is admitted on day 3 of typhoid, and her spleen cannot be felt. Around which days of the illness is it typically first palpable?
items.explanation: The spleen usually becomes palpable around **days 7–10**.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man’s fever persists after he starts a drug to which his isolate is sensitive. For up to how long can this be expected without implying treatment failure?
items.explanation: Pyrexia may continue for **up to 5 days** after specific therapy starts.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman recovered from typhoid and continues to pass S. Typhi in her stool. After what interval of continued excretion is she classed as a chronic carrier?
items.explanation: Chronic carriers are still excreting the bacteria **after 1 year**. Davidson puts this at about 5% of patients.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old man in an endemic area has had a week of fever. A local clinic reports a "positive Widal test" and labels him as having typhoid. No cultures have been taken.
questions.leadIn: What is the best interpretation of this result?
options: It is non-specific, and the diagnosis needs culture of S. Typhi
It confirms typhoid, so cultures are unnecessary
It shows that he is a chronic gallbladder carrier
It shows paratyphoid rather than typhoid
It shows that a previous typhoid vaccine failed
questions.explanation: Widal looks for antibodies against the **O and H antigens**, and a positive result is **not specific**. Kumar advises against using it at all. A definitive diagnosis needs **culture** of S. Typhi or Paratyphi, starting with blood cultures.
whyNot: Serology cannot confirm typhoid. Culture is the standard.
Carriage is shown by culture of stool or urine over time, not by Widal.
A positive Widal is non-specific, so it cannot pin down paratyphoid either. Only culture identifies whether the organism is S. Typhi or S. Paratyphi.
The result cannot be read as evidence of vaccine failure.

questions.theme: Timing in typhoid: course and treatment
questions.leadIn: Match each scenario below to the best time interval or stage in the list. Any option can be the answer for one case, several cases or none.
options: End of the second week to the third week

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman with sensitive typhoid is improving on treatment. For how long in total should her antibiotic course run?
items.explanation: Treatment should continue for **14 days**. This also reduces relapse and persistent carriage.

items.stem: A 61-year-old chronic carrier asks how long the traditional ciprofloxacin course for carriers lasted.
items.explanation: Chronic carriers were formerly treated with **ciprofloxacin for 4 weeks**. The drug and duration may now be guided by sensitivity testing.

items.stem: A 21-year-old man with untreated typhoid develops sparse, blanching rose-red spots on his upper abdomen. At which stage of the illness do these usually appear?
items.explanation: Rose spots appear at the **end of the first week**.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman with typhoid develops melaena from ulcerated Peyer’s patches. At which stage of the illness does this complication typically occur?
items.explanation: Davidson places bleeding and perforation from the **late second week into the third week**. Kumar says usually week 3.
